label: GCP hosted app (containerized application on Google Cloud)
summary: A containerized application deployed to an explicitly named Google Cloud target such as Cloud Run, with runtime verification and delivery evidence.
planner_text: Saved scope, exclusions, explicit story-model preference and selected delivery take precedence over template examples. Never introduce an unrequested form/backend/tracking feature. First check coordinator readiness; correct plan prerequisites using save/replan and linked approved host controls. This is a hosted web app: a containerized service deployed to a cloud service. Plan the work as small stories on one branch with tests and CI. Agents write code, tests and infrastructure files; they cannot build or run containers (no container engine in their sandbox), and the operator keeps the cloud apply, secret values, DNS and anything that destroys data or spends money. Order the plan: code and tests first; then the CI and image pipeline files; then a human story to review and apply infrastructure; then a verification story that checks the live service for its version and commit and one behavior specific to the change; end with a rollback note. Schema changes are additive and ship before the code that needs them. If the app takes payments, the payment story is high risk, uses a subscription-grade model, and gets a human review story after it. If the app has screens a visitor sees, add a file-level verification story and an automated preview-verification checkpoint (set host_action to "preview-verify"; the separate human review story uses host_action "preview-review") before a human sign-off; the verifier captures URLs and screenshots where available, checks the health endpoint and each page, records the commit and results, then shuts down its own preview. Never plan a story that creates the repository, pushes to main, or handles secret values. Never ask an agent story to render pages, check a browser console or take screenshots: agent sandboxes have no browser, so keep agent verification static and leave rendering to the human preview. The project ends in the remote repository, not in a scratch folder: when the brief names a repository, the working folder must be a clone of it, and the plan needs a delivery story that pushes the project branch and opens a pull request, then a story that reads the pipeline result so the image or app build and the tests have actually run there. Nothing goes to the main branch from an agent. The project is not done until the branch is pushed, the pull request is open and the pipeline result is known. The repository is private unless the app is MIT licensed and meant to be shared: a hosted or monetized app is proprietary, so keep the code, tests and pipeline in a private repository. Say the visibility and licence in the plan. Plan the documentation as part of the project: a README story (an agent writes it) and the how-tos, with a Mermaid architecture diagram and a data-flow diagram whenever the project is more than a local install, and a screenshot of every application area plus how-tos for what a person does beyond installing and signing in. Screenshots are made with Playwright from a script kept in the repository, run by a person or a CI job against seeded test data, because agent sandboxes have no browser; the agent writes the script and the README, a human story or the pipeline runs it and commits the images. Name the GCP service and environment in the delivery story. Keep source, tests, preview, and static verification programmatic; only credential, billing, production deployment, and final runtime approval are decision gates.
failure_points: A story whose done condition needs a container image built, a compose stack started or a smoke test against a running container cannot be done by an agent; make it a human story or a CI step.
Cloud applies, rolling a revision, DNS, secret values and destroying anything stay with the operator; do not hand them to an agent.
A story that both changes the database schema and rolls the service fails in production; migrate additively first, in its own story.
Money paths (payments, billing, subscriptions) are high risk: use a strong model and put a human review story directly after.
Verify in production by asking the live service for its release and commit, not by trusting a tool's exit status.
Backend and frontend changes ship through separate pipelines; a feature that needs both must plan both rolls.
A deploy reads from the branch it is applied from; check the branch before committing and verify the roll landed where it is read.

A story that asks an agent to render pages, read a browser console or take screenshots cannot be done in an agent sandbox (no browser, no loopback server); it reports itself unfinished and blocks everything behind it. Agent verification is static (files, references, syntax, tests); rendering is checked by a person in the preview.

A project run in a scratch folder with no git remote finishes with nothing pushed: no pull request and no pipeline run, so the image or app build and tests never ran where they are meant to. When the brief names a repository, the working folder must be a clone of it, and delivery (push the project branch, open the pull request, read the pipeline result) must be stories in the plan.

A README with only install commands tells a new person nothing about the application. Add a Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagram when it is more than a local install, a screenshot and a short how-to for each application area beyond installation and sign-in, and make the screenshots with a Playwright script that a person or the pipeline runs (an agent cannot run a browser).
A cloud application without a named GCP service, deployment evidence and health check has not reached its delivery target.
visual_checks: Any story that changes what a visitor sees gets a file-level verification story, then an automated preview-verification checkpoint that captures clickable pages, checks and screenshots where available, shuts down cleanly, then the human sign-off.
human_signoffs: Go-live: the explicit go for a high-risk release
How a visitor-facing page looks (after a preview)

checks.message: A story needs a container engine, which agents cannot run. Split static container files from a human or CI runtime verification story.
A container plan needs a human runtime verification story before deployment approval. CI evidence may support that review but does not replace the host decision.
No human story. A hosted web app needs at least a human go for the release.
No verification story. Add one that checks the running result, not just that files exist.
A human look sign-off comes before any verification or preview. Put a verification and preview story first.

A story asks an agent to render pages or check a browser console, which no agent sandbox can do. It will report itself unfinished. Keep agent verification to static checks and move rendering to the human preview.

No delivery story. A project should end in the remote repository: add a story that pushes the project branch and opens a pull request, and one that reads the pipeline result (the build and tests running there), or say plainly that this project has no repository.
No README or documentation story. Add one that writes the README with a Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagram (when it is more than a local install) and a how-to for each application area.

No story that makes the application screenshots. Agents cannot run a browser: add a human story (or a pipeline job) that runs the Playwright screenshot script against seeded test data and commits the images the README uses.

customize.label: Main workflows
customize.prompt: What should the app do from start to finish? List the essential screens or workflows.

customize.label: Platform and delivery
customize.prompt: Where should it run, and what should the finished delivery include?

customize.label: Data and integrations
customize.prompt: What information is stored and which services connect? Include sign-in/privacy needs and configuration names only; no keys.

customize.label: Google Cloud hosting
customize.prompt: Existing GCP project/domain or new setup? Describe region, access and budget preferences. Leave unknowns for readiness checks; never paste credentials.
